newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ANALYSIS-Singapore refining cuts may not help.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-Singapore refining cuts may not help.

text.p: Raj Rajendran

Oil giant Exxon Corp became the first Singapore refiner to cut output because of refining losses and others are expected to follow, but traders say the cuts might not be enough to help the bottom line.
Unless a fresh round of buying emerges from the region's bigger markets, such as China and India, the output cuts will not amount to much, they said on Wednesday.
Sources close to Esso Singapore said on Tuesday the company had cut output by 10 percent at its 230,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery. The company declined to comment.
Since mid-May, Singapore refiners have incurred losses averaging about 50 cents per barrel on basic refining, compared with profits of more than $2.00 in April.
As the swing factor in Asian refining, Singapore -- with a refining capacity of 1.3 million bpd -- is seen as the bellweather for the state of the industry in the region.
Weak margins in January sparked a round of cuts by the Singapore refiners. Production was down for around a month
But traders said this time around, the market was in a more precarious position.
The slump in profits has been largely the result of massive regional imports of high value petroleum products like diesel and naphtha from the West.
More than three million tonnes of diesel and one million tonnes of naphtha flowed into Asia, taking away regional refiners' traditional markets.
The imports cut diesel and naphtha prices about 15 percent between March and the end of May. Singapore diesel stands around $25.00 per barrel and naphtha at around $22.90.
The fall in the prices of these key products coincided with a big increase in crude prices, further squeezing refiner's profit margins.
"For margins to improve, China and India need to come out and buy in a big way," one refining source said.
But, for the time being, that is unlikely.

China halved its monthly diesel imports in April to 340,000 tonnes after importing at twice that rate in the first quarter of 1997, custom figures showed. The lower Chinese imports were viewed by some as a positive sign.
"The Chinese need some time to soak up their aggressive first quarter buying and if this is done in April then it is very good as they will come back to buy in July," one refining source said.
The Chinese had imported 2.06 million tonnes of diesel in the first quarter -- twice the normal import rate.
But the port congestion those imports produced meant China was likely to keep imports moderate in the second quarter, the sources said.
A similar reduction in imports was also seen in India where the state-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) bought a paltry 270,000 tonnes for June delivery compared to the 870,000 tonnes it bought for May.
Traders said IOC was not expected make a bumper award for July, with most forecasting purchases of under 400,000 tonnes. The tender for July delivery cargoes will be awarded on Thursday.
The two big Asian buyers aside, second-tier buyers such as Japan and Indonesia are also unlikley to raise imports significantly in the near future.
Indonesia has reduced its monthly imports by about 20 percent to around 350,000 tonnes due to higher domestic refinery operations.
Japanese purchases have slowed following a considerable rise in stocks of products such as diesel and kerosene.
Refiners are hoping that the poor demand will be offset by scheduled shutdowns of five crude units in South Korea in June and July.
But most feel that any cut in Asian output will amount to nought if a new round of arbitrage exports hits the market.
"It is good to know that the European refiners are also thinking of run cuts. This means that they won't dump their product here," a refining source said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3093)
